You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC notes: task-2d96d5f6

Observed demos indicate horizontal/vertical border stripes emit perpendicular rays, selecting alternating cells along each stripe (every other cell, starting at the stripe's first cell). Rays continue across the interior in the stripe's color? More precisely, demo 3: background=1; top border segment color 8 at row0, cols0-4, bottom border segment color8 at row10 cols6-10. Output emits vertical rays of background color 0 from the top segment at cols0,2,4 down all rows, and from bottom segment at cols6,8,10 up all rows. Input zeros lying on these rays become 4 (r3c8, r3c10, r5c6); other cells remain unchanged. Border stripe itself remains intact. This suggests ray color is the background color and collision marks a 0 as 4. The tested grid had background 2, border color1; top segment row0 cols0-6, bottom segment row5 cols13-19; zero markers at r2c18 and r3c14. Likely rays from top cols0,2,4,6 downward and bottom cols13,15,17,19 upward, with neither zero marker aligned (bottom segment parity is relative to its start), so both dots remain unchanged. HOWEVER, all submitted candidate grids were marked incorrect; no correct output was learned. Do not treat this last extrapolation as verified.

Other demo evidence:
- Demo 1: bg0; border color6 vertical segments at left rows1-2 and right rows3-4; interior color8 dots at r1c5,r2c6. Output connects horizontal rows to stripe, colors intervening background with 8, changes dots to4. Opposite side rows3-4 filled with8 toward other side.
- Demo 2: bg0; color8 vertical stripe at right rows0-1 and left rows2-3; interior 7 at r2c16. Output row0 c0..25 becomes7; row2 c1..15 becomes7 and marker becomes4; suggests line projection/stripe-marker rule, not fully understood.
- Demo 4: bg3; border stripe8 top c7-10 and bottom c0-3; interior 9 markers r2c7,r11c9,r13c10. Rays/fills of 9 appear from stripes and dots become4; exact direction pattern not fully resolved.
- Demo 5: bg9; color0 vertical stripe left rows5-8 and right rows9-12; color5 dots r5c3,r7c13,r8c11. Outputs show horizontal color5 fills on dot rows between border and marker, with marker replaced by4; also portions of the opposing stripe's rows receive color5. Unclear exact all-row rule.
- Demo 6: bg8; color2 border segments top-left col0 rows0-2 and right col17 rows6-8; interior 7 at r6c3,r7c7. Horizontal rays of7 project from dots toward right border, dots become4, and top boundary segment projects 7 across top rows, indicating perpendicular propagation from stripe/dots.

Operational lesson: carefully preserve exact input dimensions (and verify every row length) before submitting. All candidate submissions in this instance were incorrect; some were reported invalid-grid. Avoid overconfident guesses; demos are valuable for disambiguating stripe phase and ray direction.
